etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English heren, from Old English hīeran (“to hear”), from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną (“to hear”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti (“to be sharp-eared”), from *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”) + *h₂ows- (“ear”) + *-yéti (denominative suffix).

definitions.definition: (intransitive, stative) To perceive sounds through the ear. [from 10th c.]
(transitive, stative) To perceive (a sound, or something producing a sound) with the ear, to recognize (something) in an auditory way. [from 10th c.]

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: Mr. Cooke at once began a tirade against the residents of Asquith for permitting a sandy and generally disgraceful condition of the roads. So roundly did he vituperate the inn management in particular, and with such a loud flow of words, that I trembled lest he should be heard on the veranda.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To exercise this faculty intentionally; to listen to. [from 10th c.]

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, John:
quote.text: Agayne there was dissencion amonge the iewes for these sayinges, and many of them sayd: He hath the devyll, and is madde: why heare ye hym?

quote.citation: 1935, George Goodchild, chapter 3, in Death on the Centre Court:
quote.text: It had been his intention to go to Wimbledon, but as he himself said: “Why be blooming well frizzled when you can hear all the results over the wireless. And results are all that concern me. […]”

definitions.definition: (transitive) To listen favourably to; to grant (a request etc.). [from 10th c.]
(transitive) To receive information about; to come to learn of. [from 10th c.]

quote.text: Adam, soon as he heard / The fatal Trespass don by Eve, amaz'd, / Astonied stood and Blank  […]

quote.citation: 2009, Elsa T. Aguries, The Pearl Within, →ISBN, page 141:
quote.text: When I don't hear from you, My days feel long and lonely.

quote.citation: 2012, Art Wiederhold, Charles Sutphen, From the Depths of Evil, →ISBN, page 343:
quote.text: They're ten hours overdue. Have you heard from any of them since they left Nineveh?

quote.citation: 2012, James Meredith, A Mission from God: A Memoir and Challenge for America, →ISBN:
quote.text: She left and I never heard from her again.

definitions.definition: (transitive, law) To listen to (a person, case) in a court of law; to try. [from 12th c.]
(transitive, informal) To sympathize with; to understand the feelings or opinion of.
